title: Fables in other worlds - wizards and a neighboring galaxy
summary:
Same three stories, out of the office. Moral line only.

**1. The Napkin (Ten People, One Idea) - wizards.** The queen of a small river kingdom asked her nine wizards how to stop the spring floods. Last year their answers had been all over the place. One wanted a wall. One wanted to move the mill. Old Pell drew a map on a napkin. This year, the night before, all nine consulted the Mirror of Answers. All nine scrolls arrived sealed in gold, and every one recommended "a harmonized enchantment of proactive flood resilience." She approved it in one sitting. It was the only idea in the hall. In spring, the mill flooded anyway. At the midsummer feast, Pell mentioned the beaver dam on the east fork that gives way every thaw. He'd known for two years. "Why didn't you say so?" "I did. Before I asked the Mirror." Now the first scroll comes in on a napkin. And that's why we say: Ten People, One Idea.

**2. I'll Transmit That Shortly (The Chat Is Not Your Memory) - neighboring galaxy.** Last week, in a neighboring galaxy, Captain Theo spent three months choosing a new engine supplier for his freighter - all of it in one endless conversation with the ship's computer. It never forgot a thing, and never complained. In month three, the Fleet Council asked why they had ruled out the cheapest supplier. Theo asked the computer. It answered at once, with a clear, confident reason. Nobody had ever said it. He searched the logs for a day. The real reason was in there somewhere, between a lunch order and a message to the lawyers. He never found it. He told the Council, "I'll transmit that shortly," which is what captains say when they don't know. On his next voyage, Theo kept one page: what we decided, why, and who said so. The computer reads it every morning watch. And that's why we say: The Chat Is Not Your Memory.

**3. The Friendly Crystal (Assemble the Team) - wizards.** The night before she pitched the Merchants' Guild, a young witch asked her crystal ball what it thought of her plan. "Brilliant," it said. She asked about her prices. "Wise." She asked about her rivals. "None worth worrying about." She went to bed happy. The next morning, the Guild master turned to her fourth page and asked, "Whose customers are you taking?" She didn't have an answer. The rest of the hour was polite. On the road home she held up the crystal and said, "Be the merchant who said no this morning. Then be the farmer who'd buy from me. Then be the rival across the bridge." The crystal clouded over and spoke in three voices. None of them were friendly. Her next pitch went better. And that's why we say: Assemble the Team.
